canberra.title: Generational turn: Tech-sector growth powers Territory’s economic future
canberra.snippet: The launch of a new $50 million applied technology venture capital fund and Canberra Innovation Network (CBRIN) nearing a billion-dollar ...
canberra.content:
New Significant Ventures partner Rob Snow with founder Fiona Hindmarsh. AI is driving new opportunities. Photo: Significant Ventures.

The launch of a new $50 million applied technology venture capital fund and Canberra Innovation Network (CBRIN) nearing a billion-dollar contribution to the ACT economy over the past decade have been hailed as a coming of age for the Territory’s knowledge-based industries.

Chief Minister Andrew Barr said the investments reflected confidence in Canberra’s innovation ecosystem and its capacity to generate world-leading businesses.

“Canberra is increasingly proving that great research can become great businesses,” Mr Barr said.

“The combination of new venture capital, growing private sector confidence and a strong pipeline of innovative companies is helping drive economic growth, create high-value jobs and build the industries that will power our future prosperity.”

Government-supported CBRN has now injected $900 million into the local economy in the past 10 years.

Significant Ventures, with links to two of Canberra’s most prominent families and success stories such as Seeing Machines, has also launched its fourth fund.

It is aimed at taking locally grown innovation into industry and defence markets, building on the success of previous funds which elevated pioneers including Visionary Machines, Liquid Instruments, Partington and InstaClustr into the applied technology mainstream.

Mr Barr cited Liquid Instruments, along with other Canberra successes, Quantum Brilliance, Skykraft and Seeing Machines, in highlighting what was possible when research excellence was matched with entrepreneurial ambition and access to capital.

Other firms worth noting are Trellis Data, whose co-founders Rachel and Michael Gately were presented with the 2026 ACT Chief Minister’s Pearcey Entrepreneur Award, and Castlepoint Systems and QuintessenceLabs, whose success in the UK was highlighted during Mr Barr’s recent trade mission there.

“These businesses are taking Canberra-developed technology to international markets, attracting investment from around the world and creating highly skilled local jobs,” he said.

In his State of the Territory speech last week, Mr Barr said the new fund, along with the first investment by the government’s joint venture Activate Capital fund, signals a maturing market with more capital and experience behind Canberra startups.

“The results are starting to really show,” he said.

ANU spin-out Liquid Instruments now supplies technology across telecommunications, semiconductors, aerospace and defence, and raised about $70 million this year, contributing to a valuation of more than $400 million.

Quantum Brilliance also came out of the ANU, and it raised $28 million in 2025. With ACT Government support, it built three quantum computers in the ACT for the Oak Ridge National Laboratory in the US, Mr Barr said.

Chief Minister Andrew Barr says the results are starting to really show. Photo: Jasmine Thompson.

Significant Ventures, founded by Fiona Hindmarsh, has appointed investment banker Rob Snow as general partner. He is part of the high-profile Snow family, which will invest in the fund alongside the Hindmarshes and data centre pioneer and CDC founder Greg Boorer.

The new fund hopes to tap into the AI-driven boom in digital infrastructure and new industries such as robotics, automation, energy systems and health technology, along with increased national defence needs.

Ms Hindmarsh told Region that the fund was seeking technology founders to back early startups that can see a problem that needs solving and then sell that solution to industry.

“That’s our sweet spot,” she said. “We’re hoping to do about 20 pre-seed-style, early pre-revenue innovation opportunities. Help them formulate their ideas, get to the point where they’ve got a really strong business case, and then invest.

“The sort of products that we like are not that complicated … the science might be complicated, but the problem they’re solving has got to be fairly understandable for it to be adopted into industry.”

For example, Significant Ventures backed an optical, engineered solution that started in autonomous vehicles and was now being applied to drone detection, but it also had other applications in the mining industry and in prison and infrastructure surveillance.

Ms Hindmarsh said the Canberra tech landscape was completely unrecognisable compared with a generation ago when Significant Ventures started.

She said there was now a consistent pattern to it in Canberra, and integral to this has been ANU, and now UNSW Canberra was expanding its footprint, as well as the ongoing support from CBRIN.

“The momentum of the companies that are coming out of the ecosystem is accelerating, the number of them is accelerating, and the speed at which they’re getting recognition and getting out of spin-out mode, properly being commercialised, and then ultimately getting really interesting customers [is accelerating],” Ms Hindmarsh said.

“And most of them … the customers, are by nature global, large corporations.”

The founding pioneers and their businesses, such as Greg Boorer or Aspen Medical’s Glenn Keys, had also matured and were now in position to mentor, invest capital and provide feedback.

“We’re really at a generational turn,” Ms Hindmarsh said.

“The demand for the types of novel technologies and novel ideas that can be spun out of universities has just gone through the roof.”

CBRIN CEO Petr Adamek said the next decade presented an even bigger opportunity than the last.

“With new investment capital becoming available, we need to help more Canberra companies move from promising technologies to commercial success, compete internationally and create lasting economic value for our city,” he said.

canberra.title: Former EveryMan vice-president accused of being a ‘prolific drug dealer’
canberra.snippet: A Canberra businessman and former EveryMan vice president has been accused of being a “prolific drug dealer” across a “...
canberra.content:
Two men were arrested when police executed search warrants at a Turner home on 7 November. Photo: ACT Policing.

A Canberra businessman and former EveryMan vice president has been accused of being a “prolific drug dealer” across a “large variety of dangerous drugs”.

Alexander James Bancroft faced the ACT Magistrates Court on Monday (9 November), where he was charged with two counts of possessing prohibited weapons, two counts of possessing suspected proceeds of crime, and counts relating to the alleged trafficking of cannabis, heroin, meth, cocaine, MDMA and ketamine.

Police searched the 35-year-old’s Turner home on Saturday, 7 November, where it’s alleged they seized about $110,000 in cash, clear bags, an electric money counter, a taser, two lighters in the shape of handguns, three phones, a laptop and a variety of illicit drugs.

Police also took possession of a BMW X5 and Audi RSQ3, which court documents stated had been bought with cash in previous weeks.

Police officers seized a wide variety of drugs and other items, allegedly from the home of Turner man Alexander James Bancroft. Photo: ACT Policing.

Mr Bancroft appeared in court online on Monday (9 November), where his defence lawyer applied for bail.

She accepted that while the charges before the court were “serious”, bail conditions could be set to reduce any perceived risk of further offending or tampering with evidence.

These included reporting to police twice a week, being under an 8 pm to 7 am curfew, and having no access to an unapproved phone.

The defence lawyer argued Mr Bancroft could default on his mortgage if remanded, and his two nights spent in custody made him “acutely aware of the situation that he finds himself in”.

Prosecutor Liam Taylor disagreed, stating the charges showed the accused had a “significant risk of re-offending” and tampering with evidence.

Regarding the seized phones, the prosecutor said a password had been provided for only one device.

“[There’s a risk] he could delete any evidence from the Cloud or access the phones from other devices,” Mr Taylor submitted.

Mr Taylor also argued further re-offending and subsequent risk to the community was possible given it appeared Mr Bancroft’s alleged offending had “gone on for some time” and that the drugs were “a means of supporting himself”.

Special Magistrate Michael Cowen questioned this argument.

“So you say he’s a drug dealer, and if he’s granted bail, he’ll continue to be a drug dealer?” he asked.

Mr Taylor stated Mr Bancroft “may” re-offend, but that wasn’t a given.

Reading from submitted court documents, Special Magistrate Cowen said it appeared the police’s case was that Mr Bancroft was a “prolific drug dealer in a large variety of dangerous drugs”, but it was unknown how long the alleged offending had been occurring.

He also stated the police documents argued Mr Bancroft would be motivated to offend again, either to repay someone else for the alleged drugs or to “recoup his losses” from what had been seized.

Special Magistrate Cowen ultimately denied bail.

A second man was also arrested during the 7 November police action.

Police said Lindon Bryce Emsley, 35, was at the Turner home during the search and he was subsequently apprehended for an outstanding arrest warrant.

His bag was searched at the ACT Watch House, where it’s alleged a small amount of methamphetamine was found.

Mr Emsley was charged with trafficking meth and joint commission theft.

He appeared briefly in the ACT Magistrate’s Court, where he applied for bail, which was not opposed.

Both men are due to reappear in court on 8 December.

canberra.title: Grieving father pleads with Senate not to gut social media laws
canberra.snippet: The father of a teenage boy who took his life after being targeted online has urged parliamentarians not to water down the Federal Govern...
canberra.content:
The Senate’s review of Labor’s Digital Duty of Care legislation is underway, with pleas for it not to be watered down. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

The father of a teenage boy who took his life after being targeted online has urged parliamentarians not to water down the Federal Government’s Digital Duty of Care legislation.

The Senate’s Environment and Communications Legislation Committee is reviewing Labor’s Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026, which recently passed the House of Representatives and was sent to inquiry before the Senate debates and votes on it.

The legislation requires social media companies to take serious measures to protect people using their platforms from harmful material.

Wayne Holdsworth lost his 17-year-old son Mac in October 2023 after the teenager became the victim of a sextortion plot.

Mr Holdsworth was one of the first people to give evidence at the inquiry, which kicked off on Monday (9 November). He said he was concerned that unlawful material standards might be removed from the legislation.

“Holistically, we need to really ensure that this opportunity isn’t wasted, that we tick all the boxes, make sure that everything is included, that we need to have it included,” Mr Holdsworth said.

“Let’s not let perfection get in the way of a really good idea and delay this for another six months.

“We really need to ensure the government does include this, but does it quickly because as every day goes by, there’s kids exposed to this and there will be kids take their life because we’re procrastinating.”

Mr Holdsworth is just one of several parents of children who have taken their own lives, or been otherwise harmed from social media bullying, who are sharing their experiences with senators holding the inquiry.

Industry experts and social advocates are also appearing before the inquiry.

Before the two-day inquiry began, Communications Minister Anika Wells urged senators to pass the bill, but said she was open to further negotiations to make that happen.

She said the industry had been operating like the “Wild West” for 20 years and needed to be regulated.

“I welcome any amendments being put by any parliamentarian that strengthen or improve these laws,” the minister said.

“We think big tech needs to be held to account, and if you build it, you should be responsible for its harms,” she said.

Algorithms and artificial intelligence tools are some of the features that will be captured under the Digital Duty of Care, which will require tech companies to do risk assessments and explain how they will mitigate against risks.

Under the proposed new laws, failure to do so will attract fines of up to $109 million.

Platforms will be forced to protect children from harmful content such as extreme violence, pro-eating disorder material and content that glorifies crime or dangerous stunts.

The legislation also gives social media users over 16 the option to opt in to algorithmically recommended content or set their follower-only feed as their default. It also bans nudify apps.

The minister pointed to eSafety’s latest annual report, which shows image-based abuse has skyrocketed as AI has advanced.

The online safety regulator received more than 9000 reports of image-based abuse.

Its annual report shows complaints have increased sharply across all schemes.

A growing area of concern is online sexual extortion, which has seen a 41 per cent increase and has devastating effects.

A recent RMIT study also found one in 15 adults has been the victim of image-based abuse.

“For too long, tech companies have been allowed to live-test their products on Australians,” Ms Wells said.

“The Digital Duty of Care will apply basic safety standards on these companies, just as we have for other products like toys, cars and food.

“Under the current framework of the Online Safety Act and industry codes and standards, we can only act after someone has been harmed by an AI chatbot or had their image stolen with devastating consequences.

“In many cases, that’s tragically too late.”

canberra.title: Fairbairn saved but will it stay a community golf club?
canberra.snippet: Fairbairn Golf Club members are relieved at the Commonwealth’s decision to spare their course, but they are not yet back in the clu...
canberra.content:
9 November 2026

Join the conversation

1

The Fairbairn Gold Course is a green buffer and popular destination for ACT golfers. It’s been deemed unsuitable for other uses. Photo: FGC.

Fairbairn Golf Club members are relieved at the Commonwealth’s decision to spare their course, but they are not yet back in the clubhouse toasting the victory.

The course is still marked for divestment, and they now have a month-long wait to see what form that will take.

On Sunday (8 November), the Albanese government, in its update to the Defence Estate Audit, announced that the 65-hectare property would continue operating as a golf course and the government would explore divestment pathways that supported this outcome.

The result is a major win for the club, which has campaigned against the proposed sell-off since the government announced in February that it intended to divest 68 Defence properties.

Finance Minister and ACT senator Katy Gallagher said the decision was based on community feedback and the site’s specific constraints.

The club argued the site was unsuitable for redevelopment because of PFAS contamination and its proximity to Canberra Airport and Defence’s live-firing range.

The question is who would buy the site if it could only be used as a golf course.

Club president Brian Depree said he would ideally prefer the government to sell the land to the club at a nominal price so it could continue as a not-for-profit community concern.

Mr Depree said that, as a development proposition, the land was no longer attractive, and operating a golf course also did not stack up unless it became a members-only operation with higher fees.

“Ideally, my preference would be that they gift it to the Fairburn Golf Club Incorporated with a caveat that it has to stay a golf club, a community golf club, and we operate it as the not-for-profit association we currently are,” he said.

That way it solved a problem for the government and the land was off Defence’s books.

Mr Depree will meet with Finance officials on 11 December to discuss next steps.

He would argue that the process needed to be one which did not mean the club had to increase its fees.

“I’m hoping they’ll come to that meeting with the outline options,” Mr Depree said.

“If you have to double the fees, it becomes a members-only, and it’s a totally different environment.

“And if you make it unaffordable, then you’re not achieving what you publicly told the world you’re going to do, which is a community golf course.”

“So there’s lots of discussions to go on, but right now we’re just happy that they’ve taken the first step and committed to at least [Fairbairn] staying as the golf club, which is great for Canberra.”

Member for Canberra Alicia Payne, who has publicly supported the campaign, congratulated the community for its advocacy to keep the club operating.

“I’ve been proud to work with the community and club management to secure this outcome with Katy Gallagher and the government,” she said.

“Fairbairn is a much-loved community facility, and I’m delighted that it will remain a public golf course for the enjoyment of Canberrans now and for many generations to come.”

The club signed a new five-year lease in July and has a 10-year development plan for the course.

canberra.title: Record turnout and plenty of new Menslink champions as Canberra steps up for its young men
canberra.snippet: A record number of business and community leaders are lacing up their boots this week to tackle 142 km for a single mission: ensuring no ...
canberra.content:
Menslink CEO Ben Gathercole says the Menslink Great Walk has arrived at a critical juncture, with services more expensive than ever to deliver. Photos: Michelle Kroll.

A record number of business and community leaders are lacing up their boots this week to tackle 142 km for a single mission: ensuring no young man in the capital walks alone through crisis.

Now in its sixth year, the Menslink Great Walk traces the picturesque Canberra Centenary Trail, starting at Parliament House and looping through the territory before finishing at Yarralumla’s Southern Cross Yacht Club.

Of the 33 participants setting out on the five-day trek, nearly half are first-timers – a milestone Menslink CEO Ben Gathercole attributes to a growing community groundswell.

“Really, that’s what our mission is: creating Menslink champions who go out into the community and create a multiplier effect,” he says.

“A person engages with Menslink, then goes out to coach their local Under 12s soccer team, and there they make someone else aware of what we do. Ultimately, when it comes time for us to ask people to commit five days to a gruelling undertaking in the name of our cause, there’s enough awareness and goodwill around the Menslink brand that it gets easier each year.”

That growing support arrives at a critical juncture. It costs $1800 to support a single young man through Menslink’s mentoring, counselling, and school programs, and operating costs keep climbing.

“It’s never been more expensive to deliver our services, and we are experiencing our highest-ever demand,” Ben says.

To keep those services free and accessible, each Walk participant commits to raising $10,000. For newcomers like Raine & Horne Commercial Canberra managing director Mark Nicholls, hitting that target required some creative grassroots rallying, in the form of a darts tournament at his local community hall.

“ACT Darts got involved, and we sold food, drink and raffle tickets, and I’m happy to say I’ve just hit my fundraising goal,” he says.

But the fundraising target is only half the commitment; the physical toll looms just as large. The cohort comprises everyday professionals rather than elite athletes, and training has demanded months of early alarms and persistent aches.

“The Walk has got me out of bed earlier in the mornings to walk my dog, doing 3 or 4 km daily, and then a bigger 10 to 15 km on the weekends. That’s when the joints start hurting, and you feel a few niggles, but having that goal for my own physical health was a great motivator,” Mark says

With departure day fast approaching, Mark has leaned heavily on seasoned participants like JJR Advisory co-founder Jim Roy, who is returning for his third lap around the capital.

“I’m nervous and excited. I’ve just been quizzing Jim on what to expect, what to pack, when and how long to take the breaks, and forming a strategy,” he said.

“Jim told me, ‘It’s the hardest thing you’ll do, but it’s also the most rewarding thing you’ll do all year’. He’s coming back for a third year running, so he must be telling the truth.”

For Jim, 51, the decision to endure the trek year after year comes down to team camaraderie and an acute sense of perspective – especially when the inevitable physical exhaustion sets in.

“Regardless of whether you’re fit as a fiddle, it’s a very mentally challenging walk,” he said, stressing the importance of breaking in shoes and staying ahead of blister care.

“I learned about that the hard way, in my first year.

“In the lead-up to the Great Walk, however, you hear from people within the Menslink ecosystem. What personally hit hardest for me was hearing from the mums of some of the lads receiving service from the brilliant human beings at Menslink. After hearing how hard they’re working to put their sons on a good path, a bad knee or a blister pales in comparison.”

The Menslink Great Walk 2026 kicks off on Tuesday, 10 November, at Parliament House. For more information or to donate, visit Menslink.

australia.title: ‘Exceedingly heavy-handed’: ACT police criticised by magistrate for Tasering disabled Aboriginal woman
australia.snippet: Exclusive: Body-worn camera footage shows woman pulled off bench and a Taser activated despite ‘putting up no resistance’, magistrate say...
australia.content:
A magistrate has criticised “exceedingly heavy-handed” ACT police officers who Tasered an Aboriginal woman with an intellectual disability during a routine arrest.

The woman, named Emma, pleaded with officers not to use the stun gun on her and told them she was unarmed during the arrest at a Canberra bus stop in January.

Police were called because of reports Emma had a knife, but she was only found to have two pairs of scissors, one of which was broken, in a nearby backpack.

Guardian Australia is not using Emma’s full name at the request of her lawyer to protect her privacy.

The court was shown police body-worn footage of the arrest, in which she is seen raising her hands immediately after officers arrived and pointed a Taser towards her.

As she pushed back against an officer who was trying to handcuff her she was pulled to the ground.

While two officers held her down another placed a Taser against her back and activated it, in what is known as “drive stun” mode. Seven officers were present at the time.

The ACT magistrates court heard in September that officers also threatened to use OC spray against Emma after she appeared to self-harm by deliberately striking her head against a police van during the arrest.

A transcript of the hearing was released by the court to Guardian Australia in October.

Special magistrate Sean Richter, a former South Australian police officer, said he found the conduct of officers “incredibly” and “exceedingly” heavy-handed, and agreed that they were aware of who Emma was and her vulnerabilities before they arrested her.

“I sometimes wonder when we lost the ability to speak to people,” Richter said.

“She’s a woman that was putting up no resistance.

“She’s sitting on the bench with her arms in the air.”

Richter said Emma was involved in a motor vehicle accident when she was 12 and received a traumatic brain injury.

He said the ACT civil and administrative tribunal described her as having a mental impairment and a neurocognitive disorder, and said she had been placed on a psychiatric treatment order.

Emma was charged with multiple offences by police in relation to the incident, but all of them except possessing a knife without reasonable excuse were withdrawn by the prosecution. She pleaded guilty to that offence, which related to the scissors in her bag, and was convicted. Emma also faced Richter on other matters unrelated to the arrest.

“I was shown the video of her arrest on the charge of possess knife without reasonable excuse. I will say this; I consider that the actions of the police in that matter were unwarranted and heavy-handed,” Richter said.

“Here was a woman sitting on a park bench putting her arms in the air. She’s clearly known to the police because one of them names her.

“It’s blatantly apparent to anyone that deals with this woman that she has a significant cognitive disorder and should be treated as such. I find it amazing that in this day and age the police reacted in the way that they did.”

In a statement, ACT policing said it “notes the comments of Special Magistrate Richter in relation to the arrest of a woman in January 2026.

“As an associated civil claim is under way in relation to this matter, it would not be appropriate to provide further comment.”

In that civil claim filed in July, Emma’s lawyer, Michael Lalor, accused one of the officers involved in the arrest of misfeasance in public office.

The officer is accused of making a series of misleading statements or omissions in police evidence that resulted in more serious charges being laid, and Emma spending 28 days in custody before bail was granted after her lawyers viewed the body-worn camera footage of the arrest.

The statement of claim alleges the misleading statements include that Emma ignored police commands, that she had “abruptly” bent down towards her bag, that she attempted to strike an officer multiple times in the face, and that she was Tasered because she engaged in a “high level of violence”.

Lalor also writes in the civil claim that it would be alleged police provided misleading statements regarding the witness who called officers saying they had seen a woman with a knife.

Police said that the civilian witness had “immediately feared for his safety and departed swiftly” after seeing Emma, but the statement of claim said police failed to make clear the man and his partner “were inside a moving vehicle with the doors locked at the relevant time”.

That witness also told police, according to the statement of claim, that “I wasn’t particularly scared, I was in a car with the doors locked, so I knew she couldn’t really stab me.”

Lalor is also alleging breaches of the Human Rights Act and exemplary damages for assault and battery.

Police have not yet been required to file a defence to the claim.

ACT police have come under repeated recent scrutiny for their use of force, particularly against Aboriginal people.

In August, the commonwealth and ACT ombudsman criticised police for failing to clearly define “racial profiling” after officers in Canberra pulled guns on an Indigenous teenager they mistook for a suspect in an aggravated burglary.

In June last year, the ACT ombudsman found that in about a third of cases it reviewed, unprofessional behaviour by officers such as impatience, aggression, foul and abusive language appeared to unnecessarily escalate situations.

This led to “use of force in circumstances where a more sensitive and trauma-informed approach to negotiation and de-escalation might have avoided the need to use force or as much force”.

As part of that investigation, the ombudsman recommended that police identify and implement measures to better equip its officers with a greater understanding of “mental illness and how it affects a person’s behaviour and ability to comply with directions”, but police did not accept the recommendation.

australia.title: There’s more than a whiff of politics to the sudden call to slash Labor’s green energy subsidies
australia.snippet: EVs and home batteries are in Treasury crosshairs despite a better economic case for scaling back nuclear-powered submarines and diesel f...
australia.content:
As Jim Chalmers, the treasurer, comes under increasing pressure to fight inflation by slashing spending in the mid-year budget update, the drumbeat is loudest for cuts in one specific area: green energy subsidies for households.

Receiving the most focus is the cheaper home batteries program, which from July last year has offered a taxpayer-backed 30% rebate to households and businesses.

The scheme has become a victim of its own success. Treasury officials originally estimated it would lead to a million new batteries by 2030 at a cost of $2.3bn. The latest estimate is more than triple that figure, and only after a tweak to the policy.

Also in the crosshairs is the 2022 electric vehicle subsidy, which exempts workers from fringe benefits tax when they lease an EV through their employer and has proved more popular – and expensive – than predicted.

Despite reports that Treasury is pushing for cuts to the home battery scheme, the argument has hardly been made.

There is more than a whiff of politics to the sudden and urgent need to do away with clean energy programs, against, say, scaling back billions of dollars in diesel fuel rebates for miners.

When budget experts are asked broader questions about the big pressures on the federal government’s finances, rarely do they cite handouts for home batteries or tax breaks for electric vehicles.

In a speech on Monday, Angus Taylor, the opposition leader, again promised to “abolish Labor’s ideological climate bureaucracy” as part of his promised $31bn of budget savings over four years.

Meanwhile, the Albanese government’s recent efforts to apply an income test to private healthcare rebates for over-65s was met with howls of protest from the Coalition.

As Stephen Bartos, an economics professor at the University of Canberra, says, in all this talk about cutting spending, “nobody is mentioning nuclear-powered submarines”.

Bartos, a former deputy secretary at the Department of Finance and New South Wales parliamentary budget officer, says if the challenge is to close the budget deficit, then green subsidies “shouldn’t be their first port of call”.

“Partly because it’s small beer compared to the big-ticket items like health, NDIS and defence. But also because there is a rationale for green subsidies, if a declining one.”

The national disability insurance scheme, for example, was expected to cost nearly $54bn in 2025–26, which has made reining in the cost of the scheme an existential question for the government’s fiscal plans. In 2023, the Parliamentary Budget Office estimated the total cost of acquiring nuclear-powered submarines under the Aukus agreement to be as much $368bn over the life of the program.

The federal fuel tax credit scheme, which mainly helps major global mining companies, costs about $11bn a year and is rising fast.

Bartos is critical of government tax breaks for electric vehicles, but says the case for public support for batteries is stronger.

“I would probably be looking at where the price signals encouraging adoption [of clean energy] are weakest, and that’s probably batteries. For EVs, people are shifting no matter what.”

The case for the cheaper batteries scheme has also been undermined by Treasury officials’ abject failure to predict how popular it would be. A month into the program and it was already obvious they had got it wrong, as the expected cost blew out towards $14bn.

Not only was our appetite for subsidised batteries way higher than official forecasts, the original design of the scheme made it more desirable to buy bigger, more expensive batteries.

There has since been a tweak to the design to account for that second issue, which is how Treasury now predicts – for what it’s worth – that the program will cost $7.2bn.

These cost blowouts have amplified derision of the home batteries as “middle-class welfare” of the worst sort.

Alison Reeve, the director of the energy and climate change program at the Grattan Institute, understands the concerns, but says the evidence to back that claim “is pretty thin when you look at where the batteries are being installed”.

Notably, this is in homes across outer suburbia, such as western Sydney, and in regional areas. In other words, not in enclaves of the comfortably well-off.

Then there is the bigger-picture issue: that we risk sacrificing long-term clean energy goals in the name of short-term fiscal objectives.

“Batteries are going to be a big part of our energy future,” Reeve says. “We do need to do some stimulating of that industry until it can stand on its own two feet.”

Slashing support for batteries would damage the burgeoning web of small businesses, suppliers and tradies who have invested in servicing the infant batteries industry.

That’s not to say there are ways to improve the cost and benefits trade-off in the home batteries program. This could be by ensuring subsidised batteries deliver a community benefit by contributing to the power grid in times of need.

“We need to make sure we are maximising the public benefit, rather than just the private benefit,” Reeve says.

There are lessons in how Western Australia has designed its home batteries support scheme.

“If you look at the west coast, you couldn’t get the state subsidy unless you linked yourself up to a virtual power plan run by the network operator. That was in order to benefit the whole network,” she says.

“We also need a clear path out of the subsidy so it doesn’t grow uncontrollably.”

australia.title: These Australian ‘forest fairies’ have all but disappeared from the wild – now they have a new neighbourhood
australia.snippet: Exclusive: With only a handful of lowland Leadbeater’s possums left in Victorian forests, conservationists hope a bespoke sanctuary will ...
australia.content:
With just 13 animals left, time was running out for the Leadbeater’s possums at Yellingbo conservation area.

The critically endangered forest sprites have exacting habitat needs. They prefer cool, wet and dark forest, with large old trees to nest in and a dense thicket of paperbarks and tea trees to dart and hide in.

That type of habitat is vanishing thanks to the legacy of state logging and bushfires.

“These are not your garden variety possums,” says Dr Dan Harley, a senior ecologist at Zoos Victoria, who has worked with the species for decades.

Gecko-toed and acrobatic, they’re sometimes called “forest fairies” for the enchanting way they silently spring between branches at night, dancing in and out view.

“You can imagine them in Tolkien’s Middle-earth,” he says.

The small, soft and nimble creatures are Victoria’s animal emblem, and exist almost entirely within the state, apart from a recent detection over the NSW border in Kosciuszko national park. The species is made up of two genetic groups: a feistier highland subspecies, and the smaller, more docile lowland possums, found only at Yellingbo.

  • Sign up to get climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s Clear Air column as a free newsletter

The conservation area, located about 50km east of Melbourne, represents the last tiny remnant of a threatened ecological community known as sedge-rich eucalyptus camphora swamp – a forest type that was once widespread in Victoria, but is now nearly gone. Along with the possums, this patch of swampy forest is core habitat for the state’s bird emblem, the critically endangered helmeted honeyeater.

But at Yellingbo, the last lowland possums have been in steep and ongoing decline. From more than 110 individuals recorded in 2003, numbers dived to 20 to 30 individuals over the past decade. This year, ecologists have been devastated as nearly half of the remaining possums disappeared between October and June – thought to have been taken by predators.

As the situation unravelled, Zoos Victoria ecologists made the painful decision to intervene, evacuating the remaining possums to Healesville Sanctuary.

“We made the decision to extract all of the wild possums out of Yellingbo. So there was a few weeks where effectively they were extinct in the wild,” Harley says.

Their time in captivity was only ever meant to be temporary, while finishing touches were put on new digs at Haining Farm designed to keep the possums safer. In late October, nine possums (six lowland, two highland and one hybrid) were released into the specially developed refuge, withmore set to move in during 2027.

Eight years ago – but not a moment too soon – Parks Victoria began growing a bespoke forest for Leadbeater’s on cleared farmland, situated at the confluence of the Yarra and Don rivers. Parks, together with Greening Australia, government and community partners, hand-planted 900,000 trees, shrubs and grasses, restoring the floodplain and recreating the cool and wet conditions required for possums to thrive.

Crucially, a 3.6km fence was installed, designed to allow bushwalkers and picnickers in but keep foxes and feral cats out.

The possums have been released in pairs and trios. Leadbeater’s possums are serial monogamists and fiercely territorial. “Every group is a household and we’re trying to build a neighbourhood,” Harley says.

In the wild, the possums are “trunk lickers”, he says. They feed off honeydew and sap from smooth-barked eucalypts and acacias, like lollipops, leaving behind their signature mark, a super sticky, bubbly saliva. A steady diet of beetles, spiders and crickets provide protein.

But Haining Farm is still a young forest, with unknown food resources and without the ancient tree hollows needed for possum dens. So the zoo has installed supplementary feeding platforms, nest boxes, and fashioned branches into possum runways, turning each release site into a miniature treetop village.

On its own, the conservation area will not be enough to save the subspecies. Harley estimates at least 220 hectares of suitable habitat is required to support the lowland subpopulation.

“We’re searching for solutions in altered landscapes where threats remain,” Harley says. “The pathways are not straightforward.”

Until its rediscovery in the 1960s, Leadbeater’s possums were thought extinct. Today the species teeters on a precipice due to the historic and ongoing loss of large, hollow-bearing trees, which is also driving declines in the highland population.

Prof David Lindenmayer, from the Australian National University, who has studied Leadbeater’s possums for more than 40 years, says the dire situation at Yellingbo was foreseeable and preventable.

He singles out the state government’s failure to create the Great Forest national park – a proposed national park in the tall, wet ash forests of the central highlands, the leadbeater’s stronghold – for criticism. It is the most important action to protect the species, he says.

Despite promising to “deliver the largest expansion to our public forests in our state’s history”, Lindenmayer says the Labor government has “done absolutely nothing in terms of increasing the amount of national parks in a substantive way”. But, heading into the state election, the approach of the other parties is no better, he says.

“This is the state’s faunal emblem, and if you can’t support one of the most important species for the state, then what hope have you got?”

world.title: Collision of two trains in Egypt kills at least seven
world.snippet: President orders prompt investigation after one train derails in collision in al-Ayyat about 50km from Cairo Seven people were killed and...
world.content:
Seven people were killed and at least 125 injured when two trains collided on Sunday south of the Egyptian capital, Cairo, officials said.

The crash occurred in al-Ayyat district in Giza province, about 50km (30 miles) south of Cairo, when a train travelling to Fayoum province crashed into the rear of a train heading to the southern province of Aswan, according to the transport ministry.

An inspection indicated that the Cairo-Aswan train had been stationary on the same track, officials said.

The health ministry gave the casualty toll, adding more than 70 of the injured were discharged after receiving treatment.

Train derailments and crashes are common in Egypt, where the railway system has a history of mismanagement and poor maintenance of equipment. In recent years the government has announced modernisation initiatives to improve its railways.

Ayman Gamal, a resident of Kafr Girza in al-Ayyat where the crash occurred, said people rushed to the scene, pulled out survivors and called ambulances.

Gamal said he saw about 80 of the injured being taken by ambulances to hospital. Some passengers were trapped inside one of the carriages of the stationary train and died, he said.

Egypt’s president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, said in a social media post that he had ordered a prompt investigation.

Outside al-Wasta central hospital in Beni Suef province, where some of the injured were taken for treatment, survivors said passengers were in shock and struggling to breathe because of all the dust that was kicked up. Nearby villagers eventually got them out, they said.

Farha Gamal, a survivor who was inside the Fayyoum train, said she saw some of the passengers who appeared dead and others were struggling to find their way out of the car. “There were other cars that were completely mangled,” she said in an interview.

Emergency teams and cranes were dispatched to the crash site to clear the wreckage and restore train services to their normal schedule as soon as possible, the Egyptian railway authority said.

Last September, a train driver and his assistant were injured after two freight trains collided in the same district.

Egypt’s deadliest train crash was in 2002 when more than 300 people were killed after a fire broke out on an overnight train journeying from Cairo to southern Egypt.

world.title: How African philosophies inspired a new approach to staging film festivals in Manchester
world.snippet: See My World, an event highlighting the pan-African thought via film, poetry and dance, builds on momentum sparked by local activists and...
world.content:
African philosophies including exploring how lessons from the past can shape the present and near future have inspired a film festival coming to Manchester.

See My World, a day dedicated to independent creators from across the African diaspora in the north of England, will take place at the Contact theatre on 21 November.

The festival is part of See My World’s year-round programme showcasing pan-African arts, culture and events.

It reflects the determination among creatives and activists in Manchester to build on the legacy of the 1945 Pan-African Congress in Manchester – which connected luminaries of postwar independence movements with a shared vision of liberation – after last year’s 80th anniversary commemorations.

See My World’s CEO and artistic director, Tunde Adekoya, said this month’s film festival was taking inspiration from across the spectrum of pan-African thought, including the works of Kenyan writers John Mbiti, an Anglican theologian who died in 2019, and Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o, the author of the groundbreaking 1986 book Decolonising the Mind who died last year.

Both writers rejected the colonial conceit that African thought was inferior, stressed the importance of community and saw reclaiming African ways of knowing as essential to a people’s self-understanding.

While Mbiti sought common ground between African religions and Christianity, Ngũgĩ was a Marxist. He argued colonialism was motivated by cultural and economic conquest, and that European powers used language as their sharpest instrument. Ngũgĩ famously abandoned English to write in Gikuyu, a Bantu language mainly spoken in Kenya and criticised the role missionary Christianity played in colonial rule.

Adekoya said: “It’s a day dedicated to pan-African and global majority films from the north of England with exclusive premieres of documentaries we’ve been working on, which weave together expressions of liberation through art forms like poetry and dance.

“The whole idea is that it’s like a playground in search of strategies of liberation, using the festival as a way to explore different philosophies.

“John Mbiti explores the philosophy and spiritual understandings of time through the concept of Sasa na Zamani – in which the past informs everything that happens moving forward. That reflects how we constantly go back to pan-African histories to inform how we progress.”

Film-makers have been invited to submit films lasting up to 30 minutes from across genres, with no screening fees charged.

As well as submissions, the festival will feature documentaries produced by See My World. They include Homage, a “cinematic love letter to dance” that traces a culture through present-day portraits illustrating dance artists and archival material from Manchester, telling a story of joy, loss, migration, rhythm and resistance. Meanwhile, Poetic Justice explores how pan-African thought and Manchester’s poetry scene speak across decades.

Adekoya added: “The idea is that we would go against the norm of how film festivals are, because when we think about decolonisation, we think about how structures have been created to alienate and exclude communities.

“So we thought our film festival would look more at how we make film accessible and how stories that deserve to be seen get seen. Throughout the day we will have different activities, from exhibitions to explorations of our performances, discussions, Q&As, insights into directors’ processes, and workshops.

“We’ve been looking for literature and concepts that inform us and give us an understanding of who we truly are. And as works from thinkers like John Mbiti have come into our sphere, they have really emboldened us to think differently about our place in the world and what we do.”

See My World film festival runs from 2pm to 11pm on Saturday 21 November at Contact theatre, Oxford Road, Manchester.

world.title: Kenyan doomsday sect leader jailed for 200 years for murder of 190 children
world.snippet: Paul Mackenzie convicted over deaths of children and one adult after followers were ordered to starve themselves and their families The l...
world.content:
The leader of a Kenyan doomsday sect has been sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult disasters in recent history.

The sentence, comprising 100 years for murder by starvation and 100 years by direct homicide, came two weeks after the court in Kenya’s coastal city of Mombasa found the cult leader guilty of the crimes.

Prosecutors said Paul Mackenzie and his Good News International church ran ​a Christian doomsday sect whose members were ordered to starve themselves and their children to death to go to heaven before the world ended.

His accomplices threatened and beat victims to ensure they followed his orders. The emaciated bodies were found scattered in shallow graves and dumped in latrines. Some had been buried alive.

Mackenzie was arrested in 2023 after police received a tipoff, and weeks later authorities began uncovering bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest near the coast in south-eastern Kenya.

In total, more than 400 bodies have been recovered. Many were severely decomposed and only 26 could be identified.

Mackenzie denied murder charges, saying he did not force the victims to starve, but the court rejected that argument.

The Shakahola tragedy has gripped Kenya since the discovery of mass graves in the forest more than three years ago.

It raised questions about how Mackenzie was able to continue operating despite being on the radar of the authorities since 2017, when police searched his premises.

In 2019, authorities shut down Mackenzie’s church and he relocated ‌to the Shakahola forest, police said.

The case has also led to calls for tougher oversight of churches and other religious organisations in a country where religious faith plays a prominent role in public life.

Mackenzie, a former taxi driver, forbade cult members from sending their children to school and from going to hospital when they were ill, describing such institutions as satanic.

Cult members lived in makeshift homes of polythene sheeting and thatch that Mackenzie divided into areas with biblical names such as Jerusalem and Judea.

The plight of his followers began ​to emerge in March 2023, when a man told ​police his brother and wife had starved their children ​to death in the forest on Mackenzie’s orders.

Mackenzie was arrested but released on bail, after which relatives said he brought forward the date ​on which he told his followers the ‌world would end. Police rearrested him and ​started combing through the forest more systematically and began exhuming mass graves.

Last month’s judgment covered 191 deaths while investigations into more than 200 other deaths are continuing.

Justice Diana Kavedza-Mochache said in a hearing lasting more than eight hours that in some cases children were isolated and denied food while their parents watched.

Mackenzie faces other charges over the forest deaths, including those of terrorism, which he has denied.

Prosecutors said that while he was in detention he also directed the deaths of 52 people in Kwa Binzaro village, about 18 miles from Shakahola. Mackenzie has pleaded not guilty in that case.

Reuters contributed reporting

world.title: ANC faces bruising defeat in South African local elections with 80% of ballots counted
world.snippet: Former liberation movement’s share of national vote almost 14 percentage points below 2021 result The African National Congress is on cou...
world.content:
The African National Congress is on course to suffer a bruising defeat in South Africa’s local elections, with the once dominant party of Nelson Mandela falling to under a third of the vote nationally with more than 80% of ballots counted.

Wednesday’s fragmented vote marks another stage in the decline of the ANC, which has led national governments since the end of white minority apartheid rule in 1994. High unemployment, crime, corruption and poor local service delivery have all contributed to voters turning away from the party.

The former liberation movement is projected to lose its status as the biggest party in the two most populous provinces, Gauteng and KwaZulu-Natal, as parties began coalition negotiations behind closed doors. The final results are expected to be announced on Sunday.

The ANC was on 31.8% of the vote nationally, almost 14 percentage points below its 2021 local election result. The centre-right, white-led Democratic Alliance (DA) had 24.1% of the vote, while the uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) party of the former ANC president Jacob Zuma was on 9.3%.

Turnout also rose in Wednesday’s poll. The election commission estimated that 54.5% of registered voters cast their ballot, up from 46% five years ago.

The final shape of coalitions in some of the country’s biggest cities remained unclear with the final votes still being counted. Senior figures in key parties said they would talk with almost anyone, while keeping negotiating strategies under wraps.

In Johannesburg, South Africa’s commercial capital and biggest city, with 4.8 million people, voters have had to contend with regular water and power cuts, uncollected rubbish and potholes. The municipality, which has seen 10 changes of mayor in the last decade amid unstable coalitions, has admitted to a 220bn rand (£9.9bn) infrastructure spending backlog.

With just over half of votes counted in Johannesburg, the DA was leading with 40%, having run an energetic campaign under Helen Zille, a 75-year-old former Cape Town mayor. The ANC, which leads the current coalition, was in second place on 17.5%. ActionSA, a rightwing party led by Herman Mashaba, was on 15.5%. Mashaba has pledged never to work with Zille, whom he calls “racist”, something she vehemently denies.

Many of the ANC’s township strongholds have yet to report full results. The Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), a respected thinktank, has projected the DA will finish with 34%, the ANC 20% and ActionSA 16.8%.

Coalitions in Gauteng’s three city municipalities are often negotiated together. The DA is leading in all three.

The MK party, led by 84-year-old Zuma as he continues to weather and deny numerous corruption allegations, is expected to displace the ANC as the largest party in KwaZulu-Natal. Founded in 2023, it mixes socially conservative Zulu nationalism with pledges to redistribute land and wealth from white to black South Africans.

With half of votes counted in eThekwini municipality, which contains Durban, the MK had 41%, meaning other parties could form a coalition to keep it out of power. Meanwhile, the DA is projected to maintain its majority in Cape Town, despite growing middle-class anger over rising housing costs.

Voters choose a local councillor and a party, with seats allocated via proportional representation. Councillors will then have two weeks to elect mayors and form municipal governments.

world.title: British healthcare worker with Ebola evacuated from DR Congo to UK
world.snippet: Patient is ⁠in ​stable condition and will be transferred to a specialist ‘high consequence’ infectious disease unit A British healthcare ...
world.content:
A British healthcare worker with Ebola is being evacuated from the Democratic Republic of the Congo to the UK for medical treatment, it has been confirmed.

“A British citizen currently in the DR Congo has tested positive for Ebola,” a spokesperson for the UK government said in a statement on Wednesday. “The UK has well-established procedures for dealing with cases like this, and those processes have been activated … The risk to the UK public from Ebola remains low.”

The patient, whose identity is unknown, is in a stable condition and is expected to arrive in the UK on Wednesday or Thursday before being transferred in a specialist ambulance to a “high consequence” infectious disease unit, according to an official document seen by Reuters.

A humanitarian organisation sent the worker to DR Congo to help in the response to the outbreak, which is the second largest on record. It is the first case involving a British national contracting Ebola in the current outbreak.

The Royal Free hospital in London has a high-level isolation unit for infectious diseases such as Ebola; other centres are in Newcastle and Liverpool.

Ebola is a highly contagious, severe and often fatal illness. It is spread through direct contact with body fluids such as the blood or vomit of infected people, or dead bodies.

The current outbreak, declared on 15 May by DR Congo’s health ministry, has surpassed 10,000 cases, and 5,000 deaths. It is the 17th in DR Congo since Ebola was identified, was caused by the Bundibugyo virus, and has become the largest and deadliest in the country’s history. The Bundibugyo virus has no approved treatment, though vaccine trials are under way.

Since the outbreak started, it has spread to Kenya and Uganda in east Africa, while last month Nigeria confirmed a case in the capital, Abuja, after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus. She, along with a close contact, were evacuated to Switzerland for treatment.

In an interview with the Guardian last month, Dr Jean Kaseya, the director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), said the “unprecedented” spread of the Ebola outbreak meant it could reach the UK and other countries.

“We want all countries to know that they are not safe if they don’t take appropriate measures,” he said. “Each country, not only in the African region, but all continents, must now increase the preparedness level and the possibility for treatment.

“It is the first time three African regions have been affected [by Ebola]. The geographic extension of this outbreak is unprecedented.”

Other patients who have been medically evacuated for specialised care since the start of the outbreak include two sent to Germany and one to the Netherlands. Another case was reported in France in July.

British health authorities say the risk ⁠to the wider public from imported Ebola cases remains low and the NHS has procedures in place to manage suspected and confirmed infections.

There have only been four confirmed cases recorded in Britain since 1976, ‌according to the UK Health Security Agency.
